name: US Company → Latin America Expansion
overview: Expanding from the United States into Latin America — particularly Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia — offers significant advantages including substantial time zone overlap (1-3 hours difference with US time zones), a large and growing tech talent pool, and proximity that makes travel manageable. The region has become a popular nearshoring destination for US companies, especially for engineering, customer support, and back-office functions. However, each country has distinct employment laws that can surprise US companies. Brazil's CLT regime is famously employee-protective with high termination costs and complex monthly obligations. Mexico's labor environment is governed by the Federal Labor Law (LFT) with mandatory profit sharing and CFDI electronic invoicing. Colombia offers a more flexible but still regulated environment. The cost advantage is real — total employment costs are typically 40-60% of US equivalents — but the complexity of payroll taxes, mandatory bonuses (13th salary), and employment severance obligations must be factored in carefully.

entity_types.recommended: Brazil: Sociedade Limitada (LTDA). Mexico: Sociedad de Responsabilidad Limitada (SRL) for services, or Sociedad Anonima (SA) for larger operations. Colombia: Sociedad por Acciones Simplificada (SAS).
alternatives: Brazil: EOR/subco arrangement (recommended for under 20 employees due to complexity)
Mexico: Branch of US entity (Sucursal) — simpler but exposes US parent to local liability
Colombia: Branch registration for temporary projects
All countries: EOR/PEO for first 5-10 hires before establishing entity

legal_requirements: Brazil: Register with CNPJ (federal tax ID), State and Municipal registrations; mandatory enrollment in Social Integration Program (PIS/PASEP); comply with CLT (Consolidated Labor Laws) regime

Brazil: Monthly FGTS (severance fund) deposit of 8% of salary; 13th salary (one extra month's pay divided into two installments, due November and December); 1/3 vacation bonus on top of 30 days' vacation
Brazil: C-level foreign employees need a permanent visa (authorized by Ministry of Labor); work visas are slow (6-12 months). Many use local directors with permanent residency.
Mexico: Register with SAT (tax authority); obtain RFC (tax ID); comply with IMSS (health insurance) and INFONAVIT (housing fund) registrations for all employees
Mexico: Mandatory profit sharing (PTU) — 10% of pre-tax profits distributed to employees, payable within 60 days of year-end; CFDI electronic invoicing required for all payroll and B2B transactions
Mexico: Employee stock ownership plans (ESOP) and options can be structured via Mexican trusts; tax treatment differs from US — seek local advice
Colombia: Register with Camara de Comercio (Chamber of Commerce); obtain NIT (tax ID); register with social security system (EPS pension, ARL workplace risk, CCF family compensation fund)

Colombia: Mandatory 13th salary (prima de servicios due June and December); severance contributions placed in a fund (cesantias, 8.33% of annual salary); interest on severance pays 12% annually to employee
Colombia: Work visas for foreign employees require an employment contract and are typically granted for 1-3 years; company must demonstrate the role cannot be filled locally
All countries: Transfer pricing documentation required for cross-border services between related entities; compliance with local data protection laws (LGPD in Brazil, LFPDPPP in Mexico)

hiring_timeline.phase_1: First hires via EOR/PEO (month 1-2): Use an EOR to hire 2-5 employees. Start with engineering or customer support given the talent pool and nearshoring benefit. 30-60 day recruitment timeline for technical roles.
hiring_timeline.phase_2: Establish entity and transition team (month 3-8): Set up legal entity (fastest in Colombia ~2 months, slowest in Brazil ~4-6 months). Transition employees from EOR. Hire local leadership (country manager, finance/legal). Set up local payroll and benefits.
hiring_timeline.phase_3: Scale office and regional expansion (month 6-18): Grow to 15-50+ employees. Establish regional management. Consider adding a second LatAm country (e.g., adding Colombia after Mexico). Deepen compliance infrastructure (local tax, legal, HR team).

org_structure_adaptations: Nearshoring centers are typically structured as cost centers or shared service centers within the US parent, not standalone profit centers
Brazil and Mexico require a local legal representative (director or officer) who resides in-country — this is a non-trivial compliance commitment
Union presence is significant in Mexico (especially manufacturing) and Brazil; collective bargaining agreements (CCT in Mexico, convencao coletiva in Brazil) may apply by industry
Management hierarchy tends to be more formal than in the US. Titles and clear reporting lines are expected.
Spanish/Portuguese language ability in US headquarters leadership is valuable but not required for day-to-day if local management is bilingual
Legal and compliance team needs local expertise — US employment lawyers cannot advise on CLT, LFT, or Colombian labor code
compensation_notes: Total compensation costs in Latin America are significantly lower than US equivalents (typically 40-60% less for equivalent roles), but the cost structure is different. Base salaries are the primary component. Mandatory bonuses (13th salary) in most countries add 8.33% to annual cost. Employer-side social charges are substantial: Brazil 26-38% of payroll (inclusive of FGTS, INSS social security, education contribution, and other levies), Mexico 30-40% (IMSS, INFONAVIT, SAR, and state payroll taxes), Colombia approximately 30% (health, pension, ARL, SENA, ICBF, family compensation fund). Stock options and RSUs are less common than in the US but growing in tech. Benefits expectations include private health insurance (standard for professional roles), meal/food vouchers (vale transporte/vale alimentacao in Brazil, vale de despensa in Mexico), and gym/wellness stipends in larger tech companies. Severance costs are substantial in Brazil (FGTS + 40% penalty on termination without cause) and Mexico (3 months' salary + 20 days per year of service for unjustified dismissal).
cultural_key_differences: Relationship-building matters more than in the US. Business relationships are personal first. Expect longer trust-building periods.
Time zone overlap is a major advantage: Mexico aligns with US Central/CST; Colombia aligns with US Eastern; Brazil has multiple zones (BRT aligns with US Eastern for much of the year).
Communication is often indirect, particularly in Mexico and Colombia. Direct criticism in front of peers can cause loss of face. 'Yes' may mean 'I understand' rather than 'I agree.'
Hierarchy and formality: Use of formal titles (Senhor/Senhora, Licenciado/Doctor, Don/Dona) is expected. Addressing someone by their first name on day one is presumptuous.
Meeting culture: Punctuality varies — Brazil is more relaxed (15-30 minute delays are normal), Mexico is moderately relaxed (5-15 minutes), Colombia tends more punctual in business settings.
Holiday culture: Brazil has extensive public holidays (carnival, many religious holidays). Mexico also has many. Schedule major deadlines around holiday periods.
Work hours: Traditional workday in Brazil is 8 AM to 6 PM with a 1-2 hour lunch. Mexico is 9 AM to 7 PM with a late lunch. Colombia is closer to US hours (8 AM-5 PM).
Decision-making is slower and more relationship-dependent than in the US. Rushing decisions can be seen as disrespectful.
common_pitfalls: Underestimating Brazil's administrative complexity. CLT compliance requires monthly obligations (termo de rescisao, eSocial filings, union contributions) that demand dedicated local payroll staff.
Misclassifying independent contractors. Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia all have stringent tests distinguishing contractors from employees; misclassification risk is high and penalties are severe.
Not understanding Mexico's profit-sharing (PTU) obligation. The 10% of pre-tax profits applies to the Mexican entity (not global), but the calculation is complex and unions audit compliance.
Assuming cheap labor = cheap total cost. Employer-side taxes and mandatory benefits add 50-100% to base salary in some countries.
failing to register properly with local tax authorities for transfer pricing. Intra-group services must be documented and priced at arm's length or face penalties.
Neglecting data transfer regulations. Brazil's LGPD is modeled on GDPR and restricts cross-border data transfers without adequate safeguards.
Overlooking CFDI compliance in Mexico. All invoices, payroll receipts (CFDI de nomina), and tax filings must use SAT-approved electronic formats with specific timestamps.
Assuming English fluency is universal for professional roles. In Brazil, English proficiency is less common than in Mexico or Colombia for mid-level roles. This limits hiring pools.
timeline_estimate: 3-18 months depending on country and scale. Colombia is fastest (entity in 2-4 months). Mexico is moderate (4-6 months). Brazil is slowest (6-12 months due to Brazil Cost bureaucracy). Using EOR first reduces initial timeline to 1-2 months for first hires.
